text:
AI is finally destroying the call center jobs

1) Soon, every job. Yes, your job.

2) 1 in 4 US jobs are customer service

3) "Hitler rose to power after just 3 years of 25% unemployment." - Yuval Harari on why we should be concerned about AI job losses

4) @MustafaSuleyman worries about political chaos from just *1-2%* structural unemployment.

5) Unlike every other economic revolution, we won't be able to just give these new people jobs, because soon enough, AIs will be able to do THOSE jobs better/faster/cheaper too.

6) Imagine pushing a button to create 500,000 alien workers who literally work 24/7. For pennies. Yes, they're going to take all the jobs.

text:
It was the desire for optimization that brought us to this disaster. Because, this is objectively a disaster.

There is nothing that AI does that cannot be done by humans, and in a lot of cases, done better by humans. But we want everything optimized - fast, with no effort, no time "wasted".

This is the spirit of the age that many of us have engaged with and perhaps even forstered for decades now. Optimization, productivity, this greed for doing more, more, more, for fitting 50 hours in a 24-hour day. 

They say AI can have legitimate uses. I agree. But I disagree that any of it is in fact necessary, particularly given how easily it can be used to commit horrendous, evil acts. 

Sadly, human beings have given themselves over to the productivity greed and now, we will get exactly what we bargained for.

text:
「ビデオ通話でAIを見抜けたのは約半数」
と話題のTavus「Griffin」

■ 何が新しいのか Tavusによると、これまでのAIは
「音声認識→文章生成→音声合成」を順番につなぐ方式が多かった。 Griffinは、見る・聞く・会話する・映像を作る機能を1つのシステムにまとめて
同時に動かす。

■ 「48%が人間と回答」の条件 ・参加者は54人、通話は1分間 ・「別の参加者と、今年楽しみにしていることを話す」と説明されていた ・「相手は人間じゃないかも」と思ったかは、通話後のアンケートの最後に質問 ・疑った人は、最初の20秒以内に疑う傾向があった ・調査はTavus自身が実施

■ 「従来は3%未満」の中身 他社のAIではなく、Tavus自身の旧モデル（Phoenix-4.5）の数字で、41人中2.4%。
■ 「NVIDIAのベンチマークで1位」の中身 NVIDIAなどの研究者が作った評価で、
採点はAIが行う。 ・反応を返す力：3.83点（人間は3.92点） ・相手を読み取る力：3.73点（人間は4.20点） 返す力は人間にかなり近い。
読み取る力にはまだ差がある。

■ 今すぐ使える？ 一般向けには未提供。
一部のテスターへの研究プレビューのみ。 Tavus自身が「人間に、相手はAIではないと信じ込ませることができてしまう」と認めている。
 声は約10秒の音声から再現できるという。
日本でも今年3月、実在のエンジニアになりすました応募者がオンライン面談に現れた事例が報じられた。
 技術の進歩と同じくらい
「相手がAIだと分かる仕組み」
が大事になりそう

text:
🤖 AI startup Tavus has unveiled Griffin, which it calls the first "Human Interaction Model," able to watch, listen and respond to a person at the same time over live video. In a test run by Tavus, it said 48% of 54 participants believed they were talking to a real person after a one-minute call.

The demo has drawn millions of views and widespread alarm over potential job losses and scams. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) said the company is "launching us unprotected and unprepared into a dystopian world in which machines perfectly mimic humans." Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) wrote: "Gross. Nobody wants this."

Tavus pitches Griffin as "a tutor who notices when a student is struggling," a partner for rehearsing difficult conversations, or a support agent that can help a customer fix a broken part held up to the camera. Potential use cases could extend to serving as personal doctors, therapists, teachers, interview coaches, fitness instructors and cooking assistants: effectively an on-demand expert for any task where seeing what a user is doing lets it guide the user in real-time.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, who turned 85 in September, called it "INSANE" and typed: "PAUSE AI NOW."

text:
Yesterday we previewed Griffin, a Human Interaction Model capable of seeing, hearing, sounding, and looking like a human does. There have been a lot of questions, so I wanted to take a moment to share our thoughts.

By way of introduction: Tavus is a research lab focused on enabling machines to meet us where we are, and to understand the nuances of how we communicate beyond words.

Griffin, our latest model, isn’t publicly available yet. Yesterday’s announcement was a limited research preview to demonstrate what the model is capable of. With AI progressing so quickly, we prefer to share breakthroughs openly and in real-time as we work on a safe public release.

Face-to-face is how we evolutionarily communicate, it carries the most meaning and intent, and we want computers to be able to help with work that benefits from that emotional understanding, expression, and immersion. Some examples of the kinds of use cases we care deeply about:

- A tutor that can build understanding of how a student learns, see exactly when there is confusion or disengagement, and adapt the lesson to fit them.

- A health expert that can answer any questions about your upcoming appointment or prescription, at the pace you want, at any time you need, even on a weekend.

- A language coach that you can practice speaking with, that can correct your movement and pronunciation, and help build confidence to have real conversations

- Or the perfect assistant for everyone, that understands intent, knows how you work and remembers what matters.

We’re working with partners on safeguards and systems for disclosure, as well as inviting discussions with officials around wider regulation and safe use. People will always know they’re interacting with AI, while providing an interface that removes the need to ‘speak computer’.

We believe in a future where computers understand us well enough to make technology more accessible, more useful, and make us more capable as humans. That is the world we want to build, and we understand the responsibility to do so safely.

هل تستطيع التمييز بين الإنسان والذكاء الاصطناعي في مكالمة فيديو؟

في عام 1950 قدم Alan Turing فكرته الشهيرة: إذا تفاعل الإنسان مع آلة ولم يستطع تمييزها عن الإنسان، فقد نجحت في Turing Test.

اليوم تقدم Tavus نموذج Griffin للفيديو التفاعلي، وتذكر الشركة أن 48% ممن تحدثوا معه اعتقدوا أنهم يتحدثون مع إنسان حقيقي.

المثير أن الذكاء الاصطناعي لم يعد يتعلم فقط ماذا نقول، بل أيضا كيف نتحدث ونتفاعل.

#الذكاء_الاصطناعي #ArtificialIntelligence #TuringTest #AI

This is a disaster for the human race and I’ve really lost patience with the useless morons who can’t see that. An AI video chat that passes for human has no necessary legitimate applications. It will be used to scam old people out of their life savings. Lonely, mentally vulnerable people are going to form romantic attachments to people who aren’t real. Isolation will increase. Mental illness will skyrocket even more than it already has. Kids in grade school will have AI boyfriends and girlfriends. All of this will happen. And worse things we can’t even conceive at this point. People are already forming unhealthy emotional attachments to text-based LLMs. Once there’s an audio and visual component, it’s over. Millions of brains will be broken irreparably. 

The benefits of this technology, whatever they are exactly, are so vastly outweighed by the societal catastrophe it will cause, and is already causing, that you can’t even measure the two categories on the same scale. But at least this is the best thing that ever happened to third world scammers. So if you’re in that community, congratulations.

The whole point of building Tavus has been simple: talking to a machine should feel as natural as talking to a friend or coworker.

It’s hard to describe all the tiny nuances that make a conversation feel human. The little expressions. Moving around in your chair. Knowing when to speak and when to listen. The dance of it all.

Griffin is by far the closest anyone has come to a model that can capture those nuances. The first time I saw it being used, I had no idea I was watching our model rather than just a normal video call.

I’m so incredibly proud of this team and what they’ve built.

text:
Tavus gave me early access

got into Griffin-Lite as a research preview with @tavus  and @hassaanraza 

ran a live face-to-face session on the Human Interaction Model
full-duplex video to video
it listens while it talks
reacts to pauses and expression, not just the transcript

the numbers on the launch post are not vapor
48% thought they were talking to a person
previous systems under 3%
#1 on NVIDIA's full-duplex video bench

what felt real in the session:
turn-taking held when I interrupted mid-sentence
it adjusted what it said based on what it saw on my face
latency was low enough that I stopped counting the gaps

what still feels early:
Griffin-Lite is preview access, not a shippable customer stack yet
safety / disclosure rails are still being hardened before wider release
longer sessions still show small timing drifts on hard interrupts
emotional range is strong but not equally strong on every beat

not calling the next product wave here
just reporting a real early access run on the first HIM they put in front of testers

https://t.co/skakbQkH5X

text:
the idea of a “human interaction model” fascinates the hell out of me.

the tech is finally good enough for it to feel believable

for example, this one from Tavus can watch and listen while it talks, react to what’s happening, and interrupt you mid-sentence. all in real time.

as eerie as that is, i can see it being extremely useful for practice:

> job interviews where you get pushed on vague answers
> podcast prep so you can explain your ideas without rambling
> pitching your startup to a skeptical investor
> sales calls with someone who keeps challenging your pricing
> difficult conversations you’ve been putting off

you can customize the conversation by telling it what you want to practice, what your goal is, and how you want it to behave.

something like “i’m practicing a pitch. interrupt me if i start rambling, and tell me what i’m leaving out.”

just try not to fall in love with your mock interviewer lol

text:
Really impressive launch. Worth watching the full video:

Tavus says 48% of participants in a live study thought they were talking to a real person, not AI.

The company just introduced Griffin, a model built for real-time, face-to-face video conversations.

It can see and hear you while it’s speaking, respond to interruptions, and adjust its tone, expressions and movements as the conversation unfolds.

On NVIDIA’s VideoFDB benchmark, Tavus reports a generation score of 3.83 out of 5, compared with 3.92 for the human reference and 2.80 for the next-highest published system.

Griffin-Lite is initially limited to select trusted testers. Tavus says it is developing additional disclosure and safety measures before making it broadly available.

tavus gave me early access to griffin, and this is the clip i keep rewatching

someone on the call asks the AI a simple question: tell me about yourself

no feature list. no "i'm an AI assistant here to help."

> her name is ash
> she lives in brooklyn
> makes videos about pop culture
> calls herself a professional rabbit-hole diver
> offers to talk his ear off about the last of us

nobody is typing for her or choosing her gestures.
she watches and listens while she talks, so she never waits her turn.

45% of the 120 people in tavus's study thought it was a real person.

NVIDIA's video full-duplex benchmark gives it 3.83 out of 5.
a real human scores 3.92.
the next best system scores 2.80.

and this is griffin lite.
the full model isn't being released yet.

Real-time video that listens, watches, and talks at once.

text:
In Tavus's own study, 120 people watched a 90-second video call and 45% decided the person on screen was real. It was an AI. A separate 120 watched two real humans talk, and 28% decided one of them was the machine.

The company gave me early access to the smaller model it tested, Griffin Lite. The 28% is the number I keep coming back to. More than one in four viewers doubted two real people.

My read is that looking human on video has become a timing problem. People leave gaps of roughly 200 milliseconds between turns, the figure usually cited from a 2009 study of ten languages. Turn-based voice AI waits for silence before it answers, and that pause is often what gives it away.

The company describes this model as full duplex, meaning it watches and listens while it talks. It says the model can be interrupted, cut in on your rambling when asked, and notice someone walking into frame behind you.

NVIDIA researchers built a benchmark for this from 237 clips of real two-person video calls. Real humans score 3.92 out of 5 on its generation track. The company reports 3.83 for its model, against 2.80 for the best system in the published paper. It also reports responses in about 1.9 seconds, where that system took 2.8.

Humans answer in 0.9 seconds on the same test. Nearly a full second still separates the model from a person, and 45% is still under half.

Language models learned what to say. Face-to-face AI is learning when to say it.

text:
Most AI that talks to you over video is 5 models stitched together.

That's exactly why it can't hold a real conversation…

Tavus gave me early access to Griffin, a model built to fix this.

And you have to admit, from the launch video, the AI looks and talks so real!

Here's what most setups look like:

>You speak
>It turns that into text
>An LLM writes a reply
>That reply becomes a voice
>And then a face gets animated on top

All these step adds a bit of delay.

And the whole thing can only take turns.

So it can't nod while you're talking.

And if you pause to think, it assumes you're done & jumps in!

NVIDIA researchers actually studied this and found: setups like this can't produce the small cues that make a conversation feel real. It's baked into the design.

Griffin skips all of that!!

It's one model. Video goes in, video comes out.

It watches & listens while it talks. 
So it can cut you off when you ramble, let you cut it off, or notice someone walking in behind you.

On NVIDIA's benchmark (built from 237 real video calls):

A human scored 3.92 out of 5.
Griffin scored 3.83.
The next best system scored 2.80.

In other words…

Griffin is ~11x closer to a human than the next best AI is to Griffin.

It's not perfect yet.

A person replies in about 0.9s. Griffin takes 1.9s. Still the fastest system they tested, but there's a gap.

And this is the smaller model. Tavus is holding the full one back for now.

We spent years making AI smarter.

Turns out the hard part was teaching it to listen, wait & know when to talk.

What's one conversation you'd never want to have with an AI on video?
